newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia Metals--Aluminium strong, more LME gains seen.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals--Aluminium strong, more LME gains seen.

text.p: The London Metal Exchange's strong performance overnight underlined solid fundamentals in the aluminium market which have long been apparent in the Asian market, spot traders in Tokyo said on Wednesday.
"The market is very tight. Also here in Japan we don't have enough metal. This is a situation we haven't seen for years," said a trader at a major trading house.
Traders expected further price gains in London, supported by a continuous drop in world stocks that reflected strong demand, including from the United States.
The metal rose as high as $1,596 per tonne on Tuesday in London after news that LME stocks fell by 4,700 tonnes. Stocks have fallen 15.5 percent since January's peak.
"The next (LME) target should be at $1,650 (a tonne)," said the trader, who expected selling by smelters at that level.
Another trader saw the next trading range at $1,650 to $1,700 as long as U.S. demand remained healthy, although it was unlikely to rise much above $1,600 per tonne in the near term.

Japan's premiums for aluminium climbed to $85 to $90 per tonne, as Japan's sales tax increase on April 1 had so far failed to dent strong demand for cars, beverage cans and construction materials, traders said.

But some cautioned that the situation might change in June or July, as the effects of the tax increase may be felt by then. Additional aluminium shipments from Australia's Boyne Island smelter are also expected around that time.
"The premium will not rise much further, at the maximum another five dollars," said one trader. "It will then decline by several dollars."
The physical copper market was quiet, while a rise in Shanghai premiums to about $100 a tonne helped push up Japanese premiums to a notional $80 from around $70 last week.

Traders expected little demand from domestic end-users in the near term following heavy imports under the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) scheme earlier this month. End-users were also put off by the dollar's gains against the yen.

"In Japan, we feel no tightness, particularly after the imports under the GSP sheme," one trader said. "It must be tight somewhere else. Somebody in South East Asia might be buying to cover needs in China."

But many traders here are braced for a further rise in LME prices in the near term, due to an overhang of short positions taken under earlier assumptions that prices would decline after a consolidation phase.

"The situation's very tricky," said a copper trader at a major trading house. "It seems as if some brokers are controlling the (LME) stocks. You don't know what they'll do. The metal price could advance further towards $2,400 (a tonne)."
Another trader agreed, saying: "The next trading range should be $2,340 to 2,380, although I can't imagine copper would challenge the recent peak of $2,440 yet."

On Tuesday, LME benchmark three-month copper soared $59.50 to $2,348 per tonne, as nearby tightness lit a fire under the market and speculators piled in. The premium of cash over three-month metal rose to $100/105.
The unexpected surge came against the backdrop of a steady fall in the metal's warehouse stocks towards 150,000 tonnes, below the levels seen in March when copper hit $2,440.
A strike at Chile's Escondida, the world's largest copper mine, also unnerved some traders who feared it could escalate and slice production further from the current 85 percent of normal levels.
"The situation doesn't seem grave at the moment, " said one trader. "But of course, it can escalate. I'm worried."
